clue.text: Essence of local notice that Four Cups must close, it's said, for a spell

indicators.note: the pair of bras must close around the other letters, holding them between
four cups take two bras, so the word for one bra is written out twice

parts.note: a bra has two cups, so cups can be A BRA; four of them makes two bras

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its central letter, here of local

parts.note: AD is short for advertisement, a notice

explanation.surface: A pub called the Four Cups must shut, according to a local notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Four Cups' sounds like a pub name, but it means two bras, A BRA A BRA. 'must close' puts C (central letter of 'local') and AD between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The magic word is the incantation a conjuror utters when casting a spell or performing a trick.

clue.text: Massage, needing wind up, ultimately?

indicators.note: to wind something is to turn it round, so the word for massage is read backwards

parts.note: to massage is to rub

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of up

explanation.surface: A baby's back is rubbed until the trapped wind comes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wind' reverses RUB to BUR; 'ultimately' takes P from 'up'. Read whole, the clue describes rubbing a baby's back to bring up wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbing an infant's back is done to make it bring up trapped air, a belch.

clue.text: Web of pathetic lies between mariner and brass

indicators.note: the jumbled letters lie between the two letters for the mariner

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

indicators.note: pathetic means feeble or poorly made, so the letters of web of are badly arranged

explanation.surface: A tangle of sorry falsehoods spun between a sailor and military top brass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pathetic' turns WEB OF into FEWBO; 'lies between' sets it between A and B. 'lies' looks like falsehoods but it is part of the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass is British slang for money, and a modest sum of cash is colloquially some shillings (bob).

clue.text: A show of affection allowed? Bit of a nerve!

parts.note: X is the written kiss at the end of a letter
on means acceptable or allowed, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether kissing is permitted and is told it's a bit cheeky.
explanation.definitionFit: The long fibre of a neuron carrying impulses away from the cell is part of a nerve.

clue.text: An expert dropping in without it's rather tasteless

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so what remains goes round it
dropping means the letters of in are let fall from the expert

parts.note: a boffin is an expert, especially a scientist, so an expert is a boffin
it, the apostrophe-s a mere link

explanation.surface: An expert pulls out, saying the remaining offering lacks taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking: the trimmed expert goes round the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Slightly off-colour or in poor taste is an idiom for a remark that is somewhat crass.

clue.text: Mysterious character reared in the nursery

indicators.note: reared says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters sit inside the words the nursery

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A strange child brought up in the nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft left 'in' unused; it is the hidden-word signal. In a down clue 'reared' means raised upward, reading ENUR from the bottom up.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter of an ancient Germanic alphabet, carved and thought magical, is a mysterious symbol.

clue.text: Balance demonstrated using these pairs of parallel bars?

definitions.text: Balance demonstrated using these pairs of parallel bars?

parts.words: Balance demonstrated using these pairs of parallel bars
parts.note: the gymnast's parallel bars are really the two short horizontal strokes showing that both sides of a sum balance

explanation.surface: A gymnast shows off balance on the parallel bars.
explanation.definitionFit: The mathematical symbol made of two parallel lines shows that two expressions balance.

clue.text: Jones's last major hit on which nobody performed work? The reverse

definitions.text: Jones's last major hit on which nobody performed work? The reverse

indicators.note: the reverse tells us the whole string is read backwards
last picks out the final letter of Jones's

parts.note: a chart-topper is a number one, written NO and 1 as I
nobody is none
the erg is a unit of work in physics

explanation.surface: A musician's last big hit was an instrumental, with no singer working on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, it is Booker T. Jones's 1962 hit with the MGs, a famous instrumental on which nobody sang; the erg is the physicist's unit of work.
explanation.definitionFit: Booker T. & the MGs, led by organist Booker T. Jones, had their best-known chart success with this vocal-free instrumental.

clue.text: US resident regrets 'no malignancy' is showing up

indicators.note: up, in a down clue, says the hidden letters are read from the bottom
showing means the words put the answer on display within them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An American patient is relieved to hear there is no malignancy.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft gave 'showing up' wholly to the reversal; 'showing' signals the hidden word and 'up' reads it upward in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The venomous lizard native to the south-western United States is a resident of America.

clue.text: He's broken when investing in Crooks Ltd. foolishly?

definitions.text: He's broken when investing in Crooks Ltd. foolishly?

indicators.note: foolishly says the letters are muddled up

parts.note: he, the apostrophe-s a link

explanation.surface: An investor is ruined after putting money into a company of crooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foolishly' rearranges HE with CROOKS LTD. Read whole, the clue pictures someone left broke by buying shares in a crooked firm.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who owns shares in a company is an investor in it, ruined if it fails.

clue.text: Bring back into room douane's case: checking counter spot phoney operative

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside letters, here of douane's
checking means holding back or containing, so the anagram holds the reversed spot
operative suggests working or being worked on, so the letters of phoney are rearranged
counter means running against, so the spot is read backwards

parts.note: a zit is a pimple or spot

explanation.surface: A French customs officer's case examined for a fake spot at the counter.
explanation.walkthrough: Douane is French for customs, so 'douane's case' sounds like luggage. 'room' means awareness of the room one is in.
explanation.definitionFit: To wake a person from a trance is to return them to awareness of their surroundings.

clue.text: Remark wingers of Les Bleus should be red-carded

indicators.note: the wingers are the players on the flanks, the outer letters of the team
a red card sends a player off, so those outside letters leave

parts.note: the French national team is nicknamed Les Bleus, and équipe is French for team

explanation.surface: A comment that the wide players of the French team deserve sending off.
explanation.walkthrough: Les Bleus is the French national side; French for team is EQUIPE. 'wingers' are its end letters, which 'should be red-carded' removes.
explanation.definitionFit: A witty remark or wisecrack is a short clever comment.

clue.text: Spenser's easily part of Poet Heritage

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Spenser's verse is an easy part of a poet's legacy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spenser's' marks an old word used by Edmund Spenser, the Elizabethan poet of The Faerie Queene.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word meaning easy or easily, found in Spenser's poetry.

clue.text: Ailurophile's top facilitator of tunes, one shilling rings … and turkey?

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter, here of Ailurophile's
the shilling rings, encircling the other letters

parts.note: bob is old British slang for a shilling coin
one as the indefinite article a
a DJ, disc jockey, plays records

explanation.surface: A cat lover's tune-making gadget, a shilling ringing up, and a turkey for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: An ailurophile is a cat lover. Bob is pre-decimal British slang for a shilling; it 'rings' A and DJ.
explanation.definitionFit: A turkey is a flop or failure, and a botched piece of work is a failure.

clue.text: African six-footer stops drunk in Paris

indicators.note: stops as in stopping a bottle: the insect plugs the gap inside

parts.note: bu is French for drunk, the past participle of boire
an insect has six feet, like an ant

explanation.surface: A tall African man stops someone drunk in Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'six-footer' suggests a tall person, but it is an insect with six legs.
explanation.definitionFit: The large group of peoples of central and southern Africa speaking related languages.

clue.text: Your clubs, Mr Benitez, rejected another cup of tea

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
Rafa Benitez, the football manager, is known as Rafa

explanation.surface: A football manager turns down your clubs' offer of another cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: Rafa Benitez managed Liverpool and other football clubs. 'cup of tea' is British idiom for one's preference, so 'another cup of tea' is something quite different.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is very different from another uses the same idiom as 'a different kettle of fish'.

clue.text: African Tree Day no longer observed by a scientist

indicators.note: no longer observed means the day is dropped, like a holiday no longer kept

parts.note: Michael Faraday was the British physicist and chemist

explanation.surface: An African tree-planting day is no longer celebrated, according to a scientist.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall West African hardwood species, also called limba, is a tropical timber tree.

clue.text: East coast Scots bay topped west coast one off

indicators.note: topped means the first letters of both words are cut off

parts.note: Oban is a bay and town on the west coast of Scotland

explanation.surface: One Scottish bay outdoes another across the country, which is out of favour.
explanation.walkthrough: Oban is a ferry port on Scotland's west coast; 'topped' removes the O from OBAN and from 'off'.
explanation.definitionFit: A town on Banff Bay on the Moray Firth coast in north-east Scotland.

clue.text: In tears — no gal to kiss and cuddle

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone is crying because no girl will kiss them.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a passionate kiss, a session of necking.

clue.text: Back to London, whither the M1 goes further

definitions.text: Back to London, whither the M1 goes
definitions.meaning: with your back to London, the motorway runs to the north: split 3,1 as the article plus N
furthermore or besides, as in 'and, besides, ...'

explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main motorway from London to the north; read 3,1 the answer is 'the N(orth)'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adverb meaning moreover or in addition.

clue.text: Game-maker from Arab state? No question

indicators.note: no tells us that the question letter is left out

parts.note: Qatari means from Qatar, a Gulf state

explanation.surface: A games company from an Arab state, beyond question.
explanation.definitionFit: The American company famous for early video games consoles such as Pong.

clue.text: Into impersonating Elvis? Well, it's … the money

definitions.meaning: keen on or enthusiastic about something

definitions.text: impersonating Elvis? Well, it's … the money
definitions.meaning: Elvis sang Blue Suede Shoes, whose opening line is 'Well, it's one for the money'; the gap is the missing words

explanation.walkthrough: Blue Suede Shoes, written by Carl Perkins and recorded by Elvis, opens 'Well, it's one for the money, two for the show'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers gives this phrase for an enthusiast of something, just as being 'into' a hobby means loving it.

clue.text: Take me on whenever mineral collects

parts.note: if can mean whenever, as in 'if it rains, we stay in'

indicators.note: collects means gathers in, so the mineral holds on

parts.note: ore is mineral-bearing rock

explanation.surface: Take me on whenever the mineral samples are collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take me' looks like the start of a request, 'Take me on'; 'on' is in fact the piece the mineral collects.
explanation.definitionFit: Speaking personally, as an example: offering oneself as a case in point.

clue.text: Arch-playmate Eve's back's out, chit trapping the nerve!

indicators.note: trapping means the IOU surrounds the other letters

parts.note: an IOU is a chit acknowledging a debt

indicators.note: out means that letter is removed

parts.note: comedian Arthur Askey's catchphrase was 'Hello, playmates!', so he is the chief playmate

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter, here of Eve's

explanation.surface: A playmate named Eve has gone, with her IOU still holding a grudge.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Askey was a British comic whose radio catchphrase was 'Hello, playmates!'. 'back's' gives the E of 'Eve's', which 'out' drops from ASKEY; IOU then traps ASKY.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclamation of exasperation or indignation at someone's cheek or impudence.

clue.text: Not much time left to put back tracks removed (not right)

indicators.note: tracks means follows, so the other pieces come after it
not means the right letter is left out

parts.note: removed means distant, far away

indicators.note: put back means the little word to is reversed

explanation.surface: Little time is left to restore the railway tracks that were taken up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tracks' looks like railway lines but means follows: the time, left and reversed pieces come after the trimmed first piece.
explanation.definitionFit: An ironic idiom meaning very little or nothing at all, as in 'a fat lot of good'.

clue.text: Feature of last month's retro house name

indicators.note: retro means backward-looking, so the house is read in reverse

parts.note: Leo is a house of the zodiac

explanation.surface: Last month's feature was a retro house name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house name' looks like one phrase, but the house is a zodiac sign and the name is N.
explanation.definitionFit: A Christmas carol or the season itself, a feature of December, the year's final month.

clue.text: Upset building block of course loses me race for four tokens

indicators.note: upset, in a down clue, turns the course unit upside down
loses means the letters of me are taken out

parts.note: a module is a unit of a course of study

explanation.surface: An upset builder loses a race with four pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' takes M and E out of MODULE to leave ODUL; 'Upset' turns that upside down in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The board game in which each player races four counters home is a race game.

clue.text: A little revelry groups may get up to?

definitions.text: A little revelry groups may get up to?

indicators.note: get up, in a down clue, says the hidden letters are read upward
a little of the next words supplies the answer, hidden inside them

explanation.surface: Party groups may get up to a bit of revelry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get up' reads the letters in 'revelry groups' upward. Read whole, it is what revellers may indulge in.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild party with unrestrained drinking and sex is excessive revelry.

clue.text: Motor man reported by Macduie and Nevis?

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the word is as it sounds

parts.note: Ben Macdui and Ben Nevis, the two highest Scottish mountains

explanation.surface: A motoring man reported by two Scottish mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scotland a ben is a mountain; Ben Nevis and Ben Macdui are the country's two highest peaks.
explanation.definitionFit: Karl Benz built the first practical petrol car, founding Mercedes-Benz.

clue.text: Have to carry teddy?

definitions.meaning: to have, as in a tree having fruit or a document having a signature
a teddy is a cuddly toy animal

explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link here; the whole surface reads like a child insisting on taking a toy along.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to hold or support, and the noun is the animal the soft toy represents.

clue.text: Quick, hide stuff being cut in review

indicators.note: in says the shortened stuffing goes inside the review phrase

parts.note: to run over something is to review it

indicators.note: being cut means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to force is to stuff or cram

explanation.surface: A quick review of material that was cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick, hide' is an urgent command, the definition taken as a whole; 'review' needs the two-word phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A cry urging others to shelter fast, said as an imperative warning.

clue.text: Affected youth who reportedly runs a hostel by the end of the Northern Line

indicators.note: reportedly says the word is given as it sounds

parts.note: the word who, said aloud
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
YH is the map abbreviation for youth hostel

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, here of the

parts.note: RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Someone who runs a youth hostel near the end of the Northern Line.
explanation.walkthrough: The Northern Line is a London Underground line; here 'Northern' is N and 'Line' is RY. YH marks youth hostels on British maps.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud, braying, upper-class young British man, a stereotype of privileged posh behaviour.
